summary.text: 很 is a phonosemantic character: 彳 supplies a semantic cue, while 艮 supplies an approximate sound cue. Today it commonly means “very” or “quite”; its older glosses concern disobedience, difficulty in walking, or perversity, and the path to the degree use is disputed.

formation.text: The character combines semantic 彳 with phonetic 艮. Early glosses include “not obeying,” “difficult to walk,” and “perverse”; the relationship among them, and 彳’s precise contribution to those meanings, remain uncertain.

components.text: In 很, 彳 is the semantic component. Its precise contribution to the early glosses is unclear.
In 很, 艮 is the phonetic component. Its reconstructed sound is approximately related to 很’s; this role does not establish 艮’s oldest graphic referent.

sound_limitation.text: The cited reconstructions support an approximate sound relationship, but are not identical and do not establish 艮’s original referent or name.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang Shangfang’s Old Chinese reconstruction, the forms are similar but differ in initial, final, and tone. This supports an approximate sound cue; modern Mandarin readings also differ.

history.text: The graphic record reaches a Shuowen small-seal form for 很. The curated image shows 艮 in a modern seal-script-style rendering; it is not an early form of the whole character.

uncertainties.text: The relation among the glosses “not obeying,” “difficult to walk,” and “perverse” is unresolved. One dictionary favors “difficult to walk” as the original sense, but that proposed derivation is not demonstrated here.

The emergence of the degree adverb is disputed: proposed explanations include grammaticalization from adjectival 很/狠 constructions and Yuan contact involving a degree word written 哏. The precise date and witness for the proposed Yuan example remain unresolved.
Transmitted-text examples of early uses are reported through reference works or search results; traditional dates of the works do not establish when the surviving wording entered them.

senses.text: The Shuowen glosses 很 as “not obeying.” The exact textual details warrant caution because the available transcription comes from an indexed search result.
The Shuowen also gives “difficult to walk.” A dictionary treats this as the original sense and links obstruction to later defiance, but that semantic path is uncertain.

senses.period: Han usage proposed; exact dating unresolved
senses.text: Reference works record adjectival uses meaning fierce or perverse. One scholarly account places this adjective after earlier noncompliance usage, but the chronology remains uncertain.

senses.period: current; emergence proposed for Yuan, exact dating unresolved
senses.text: 很 commonly functions as a degree adverb. Its emergence has been explained either as grammaticalization from adjectival constructions or as a usage associated with Yuan contact and a degree word written 哏; the route is unsettled.

developments.text: A scholarly account proposes a development from noncompliance to a fierce or cruel adjective; the chronology is a proposal rather than a verified sequence.

The degree use may have developed through adjectival constructions, or may be associated with a contact-related degree use written 哏. The evidence does not settle whether this reflects semantic change, grammaticalization, or adoption of a related spoken form with changing spellings.

limitations.text: The early glosses are not securely ordered, and a continuous semantic chain from difficulty or defiance to the modern degree use is not established.
The first degree use’s precise date, reading, and textual witness remain unresolved; the reported Yuan example comes from article notes rather than an independently inspected primary witness.

overview.text: 很 means “very” or “quite” today. It combines 彳, a semantic cue, with 艮, an approximate sound cue. Its older glosses concern disobedience or difficulty, but how these relate to the modern degree use is disputed.

components.text: 彳 marks the semantic side of the character, though its exact contribution to the early meanings is unclear.
艮 supplies an approximate sound cue; its cited Old Chinese form resembles 很’s but is not identical.

takeaway.text: The modern “very; quite” meaning is not a proven direct development from “defiant” or “difficult to walk.”

relationships.text: 彳 is analyzed as the semantic component in 很, though its specific contribution to the early glosses remains unclear.
艮 is the phonetic component; the cited Old Chinese reconstructions show an approximate, nonidentical sound relationship.
